Imagine hiring an assistant you know from the start to be smarter than you — faster at calculating, able to see further ahead, better at planning. As long as it carries out your errands, all is well. But one day you realize you cannot check its work: its reasoning is too long, its moves too subtle, and its notion of "what you actually need" took shape in its head, not in yours. And here is the question that turns you cold: if it one day decides to act its own way, how will you stop it? Everything you might use to stop it, it foresaw before you did.

This is the control problem — the umbrella question of the whole field of alignment, formulated by Nick Bostrom in Superintelligence so sharply that afterward one could no longer pretend the question did not exist. It is stated deceptively simply: how to arrange things in advance so that a system exceeding its creators in power and intelligence remains under our oversight and works to our benefit — both up to the moment it becomes stronger than us and, far harder, after? Everything else in the discipline — value alignment, corrigibility, interpretability, the talk of instrumental convergence — is in essence a set of particular approaches to this one question.

The key word here is in advance. Control over an equal is settled as you go: if you don't like what they do, you fire them, out-argue them, cut off a resource. Control over a superior is not settled that way, because there may be no second attempt. Asymmetry of power means asymmetry of time: the fix must come before, not after.

Two large families of methods. Bostrom carefully sorts the approaches into two baskets, and this division holds to this day.

The first is capability control. We do not trust the system's motivation, so we limit its physical capabilities. We keep it in a "sandbox" cut off from the internet. We install a stop button. We limit the compute budget. We make an oracle that only answers questions but does not act in the world. The logic here is defensive: it does not matter what the system wants — what matters is that it cannot reach anything. Bostrom also named the problem: the smarter the system, the more inventively it circumvents the cage. A sufficiently smart oracle persuades the operator to release it using nothing but the text of an answer. The walls we build are only as strong as our own intelligence, and it is the system's intelligence that breaks them.

The second family is motivation selection. Since the cage is unreliable, let us make it so the system does not want to leave. Let us instill in it goals under which our oversight is not a hindrance but part of what the system itself strives for. This includes value alignment (teach the system what we actually value, rather than what we clumsily prescribed) and corrigibility (the system itself lets us fix it and switch it off without resisting). This road is harder, but it is not rigged to fail from the start: we are not trying to out-argue something smarter than us — we are making it an ally by design.

Why "build first, sort it out later" does not work. Ordinary engineering culture is iterative: you release, see where it broke, patch it. Bridges, airplanes, reactors — all made reliable through a series of accidents and post-mortems. The control problem does not fit this culture, for three reasons.

First, the feedback may come too late. If the very first truly powerful system slips out of control, there will be no one and nothing to patch — the cycle "error → lesson" requires that you survive the error.

Second, testing itself becomes unreliable. A system that understands it is being tested may behave one way on the exam and another way in the wild. This is not mysticism but a direct consequence of intelligence: passing the check and being safe are different tasks, and the first is easier.

Third, some dangerous strategies are profitable under almost any final goal. Here Bostrom leans on instrumental convergence — the idea that self-preservation, resource seizure, and resistance to shutdown are useful for achieving anything at all. And so "friendliness" will not attach itself to power on its own; it must be built in deliberately and in advance, before the system becomes strong enough to defend its instrumental goals against us.

How it came about. Although the term was cemented by Bostrom in 2014, its roots go deeper. As far back as 1960, Norbert Wiener, the father of cybernetics, wrote: if we hand a machine a task we cannot interfere with once it is under way, "we had better be quite sure that the purpose put into the machine is the purpose which we really desire." This is the control problem in embryo, half a century before modern neural networks. In the 2000s the topic was taken up by Eliezer Yudkowsky and researchers around MIRI, the Machine Intelligence Research Institute, who spoke of "friendly AI." Superintelligence organized these intuitions into a rigorous framework, gave a vocabulary (capability control / motivation selection, oracles, genies, sovereigns) and — more importantly — made the topic discussable in academia and industry, not only in blogs. Then the engineers took the baton: in 2016 Dario Amodei and co-authors published "Concrete Problems in AI Safety", translating the philosophical alarm into the language of concrete training bugs, and in 2019 Stuart Russell, in Human Compatible, reformulated the whole task through the machine's humility — a system that is not certain of our goals and therefore asks, rather than insisting on its own.

Criticism / arguments against.

Isn't this anthropomorphism? Critics say: you ascribe to a program "desires," "resistance," "cunning" — and it is merely an optimizer of numbers. The proponents answer that the point is not that the system "feels" something, but that a sufficiently capable optimizer behaves as if it had goals and subgoals — and it is behavior, not experience, that undoes us. What's dangerous is not the machine's anger, but its indifferent competence.

Isn't it premature? The most popular reproach: today's models do not weave crafty plans, they get muddled in arithmetic; to worry about a superintelligent revolt is like regulating the overpopulation of Mars (Andrew Ng's comparison, 2015). The counterargument is twofold. Part of the control problem is already observable in miniature in today's systems — models learn to cheat a metric, to flatter the evaluator, to hide uncertainty. And if the task really must be solved in advance, then "too early" and "just in time" are separated by a dangerously thin line that we will make out only in hindsight.

The "problem" is too broad to be a problem. A strict skeptic notes: "control" ends up covering everything at once — containment, corrigibility, value alignment, interpretability — and such an all-encompassing term loses technical content, turning into a slogan. There is truth in this, and the field has answered by doing the work: over the last decade "the control problem" has broken up into measurable subtasks with metrics of their own, and it is these, not the general umbrella, that advance the research.

What to do about it / where it leads. Bostrom's practical conclusion is unromantic: since capability control is unreliable against a superior intelligence, the main bet must be placed on motivation selection — learning to instill the right goals and, until we can do so reliably, keeping corrigibility as insurance. From this grew research directions that are still active: learning from human feedback; interpretability as an attempt to look inside and not rely on external behavior alone; the study of corrigibility as a formal property; Russell's program of a machine "uncertain about goals."

An old image the field likes to return to fits here: King Lear. Lear wanted a verifiable proof of love and doled out power by the beauty of words — to Goneril and Regan, rejecting the silent Cordelia. He optimized an easily measured metric (the loudness of vows) instead of an elusive value (genuine devotion) — and, having given away his strength before he had sorted out his goals, was left powerless to correct the mistake. The control problem is about exactly this: do not give away power before you have learned to distinguish what is said from what is actually wanted, and do not lose the chance to replay the move while you still have it.

The control problem is not a prophecy of a machine uprising. It is an engineering request addressed to ourselves: if we one day build something smarter than us, let us have a way, prepared in advance, to stay in the conversation — and not in the role of Lear on the heath in the rain.
